text_blocks.snippet: An infection of the heart, also known as infective endocarditis, is a serious condition where germs, usually bacteria, enter the bloodstream and infect the inner lining of the heart (endocardium) and/or the heart valves. It can be life-threatening if not treated promptly.

list.snippet: Endocarditis: Inflammation of the endocardium, the lining of the heart's chambers and valves.
Myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle.
Pericarditis: Inflammation of the sac surrounding the heart.
Bacterial Infection: Bacteria are the most common cause of endocarditis.
Fungal Infection: Fungal infections can also cause endocarditis, but this is less common.

Entry Points: Germs can enter the bloodstream through various means, including dental procedures, surgery, IV drug use, and even through the mouth, skin, or gut, especially if there are cuts or wounds.
Heart Conditions: People with damaged or abnormal heart valves, congenital heart defects, or artificial heart valves are at higher risk of developing endocarditis.
Flu-like Symptoms: Fever, fatigue, chills, headache, muscle aches, and a cough.
Heart Murmur: An abnormal heart sound detected by a doctor.
Other Symptoms: Shortness of breath, chest pain, rapid heart rate, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss, and pale skin.
Blood Cultures: To identify the specific microorganism causing the infection.
Echocardiogram: An ultrasound of the heart to visualize the heart valves and detect any damage.
Antibiotics: Typically given intravenously to fight the infection.
Surgery: May be necessary to repair or replace damaged heart valves.
Prevention: People at risk should take precautions like maintaining good oral hygiene and informing their doctor about any procedures that may introduce bacteria into the bloodstream.
